claims.text: The protective coating has a mixed FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy structure.
The baseline coating undergoes progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading.
Increasing Al content will amplify lattice distortion.
Al content can be increased without forming unwanted secondary phases.
Higher Al content produces solid-solution strengthening through enhanced lattice distortion.
Al has a large atomic radius and induces lattice distortion when incorporated into refractory high-entropy-alloy solid solutions.
Al-induced local lattice distortions create obstacles to dislocation glide.
Al-induced local lattice distortions create obstacles to dislocation climb during prolonged loading.
Impeded dislocation glide and climb reduce creep rate relative to the baseline alloy.
The increased-Al coating will have a lower steady-state creep strain rate than the baseline coating.
The increased-Al coating will enter tertiary creep later than the baseline coating.
The proposed mechanism operates at high temperatures and stresses where dislocation mobility and creep are thermally activated.
The proposed mechanism applies only before precipitation, recrystallization, or other phase instabilities intervene.
Identically tested baseline-Al and increased-Al coatings provide a controlled comparison for assessing the hypothesis.
XRD can be used to quantify the relevant lattice distortion.
TEM observations of dislocation density and arrangement can assess dislocation impediment.
A lack of statistically significant creep-rate reduction after increasing Al would falsify the proposed governing role of Al-induced lattice distortion.
A failure to delay tertiary creep or to observe increased lattice distortion or dislocation impediment would falsify the hypothesis.
